Case Study 4: Respiratory Hospitalizations and Cold Waves in the South Region

Complete SIH + INMET + cold wave pipeline | RS, SC, PR | 2014–2022

Dr. Max Anjos

20 September, 2026

Source: vignettes/ec-04-hospitalizacoes-frio.Rmd
ec-04-hospitalizacoes-frio.Rmd

Objective

This case study estimates the excess of hospitalizations for respiratory diseases (pneumonia, bronchitis, COPD) associated with cold waves in the three states of Brazil’s South Region — Rio Grande do Sul (RS), Santa Catarina (SC), and Paraná (PR) — from 2014 to 2022. The pipeline integrates weekly data from the SIH-RD (Hospital Information System) of DATASUS with automatic cold wave detection using WHO (World Health Organization) and INMET criteria, via the sus_climate_compute_coldwaves() function. The final product is a weekly dataset with cold wave flags stratified by state and age group.

Scientific Context

Brazil’s South Region has the country’s most severe thermal regime, with minimum temperatures below 0°C frequent in the highland areas of RS and SC during June, July, and August. Episodes of intense cold are associated with incursions of polar air of Antarctic origin (known locally as friagem), which affect the entire South Region and, in La Niña years, extend as far as the Center-West. During these episodes, hospitalization rates for pneumonia, acute bronchitis, and COPD exacerbation increase significantly, placing a burden on the SUS hospital system.

The biological mechanism behind the effect of cold on the respiratory tract is multiple: cold air inhibits mucociliary clearance, reduces upper airway cilia motility, increases the viscosity of bronchial secretions, and facilitates the adhesion and replication of respiratory viruses — especially influenza A/B and RSV — in airway epithelial cells (Eccles, 2002). Hospitalization for pneumonia is the clinical outcome most used in cold-wave epidemiological studies because it combines sufficient clinical severity to generate admission with a case volume compatible with statistical analysis, even during short exposure periods (Gasparrini et al., 2015).

The SIH-RD (Hospital Admission Authorization Report) records all Hospital Admission Authorizations (AIH) of the SUS, including admission diagnosis (primary and secondary ICD-10 codes), admission date, discharge date (discharge or in-hospital death), length of stay (DIAS_PERM), procedure performed, patient’s municipality of residence, and AIH cost. For studies of the impact of extreme climate events, the SIH is more sensitive than the SIM-DO for morbid outcomes — it captures the broader clinical spectrum of worsening, not just fatal cases.

The two cold wave detection criteria are complementary: the WHO criterion defines a cold wave as a minimum temperature below the 10th percentile of the reference series (1981–2010) for at least 3 consecutive days; the INMET criterion defines extreme cold as a minimum temperature below the climatological monthly mean minus 5°C for at least 5 consecutive days. The WHO criterion is more sensitive (detects more events); the INMET criterion is more specific (requires a more severe deviation from the climatological normal).

Data Used

Source System Variables States Period
DATASUS SIH-RD Admissions by ICD-10 J00–J99 (AIH) RS, SC, PR 2014–2022
INMET Automatic weather stations Minimum temperature (tair_min_c), maximum temperature (tair_max_c), dry-bulb temperature (tair_dry_bulb_c) RS, SC, PR 2014–2022
SIH vs. SIM-DO: The SIH records hospital admissions (severe morbidity), while the SIM records deaths (mortality). Admissions are more frequent and capture clinically relevant cases that do not progress to death. For cold events, which cause more admissions than direct deaths, the SIH is the more appropriate system.

Complete Pipeline 

library(climasus4r)

# --- 1. Health — SIH hospitalizations for respiratory diseases ---
df_saude <- sus_data_import(
  uf     = c("RS", "SC", "PR"),
  year   = 2014:2022,
  system = "SIH",
  lang   = "pt"
) |>
  sus_data_clean_encoding(lang = "pt") |>
  sus_data_standardize(lang = "pt") |>
  sus_data_filter_cid(
    disease_group = "respiratory",
    lang          = "pt"
  ) |>
  sus_data_create_variables(
    create_age_groups    = TRUE,
    age_breaks           = c(0, 18, 50, 65, Inf),
    age_labels           = c("< 18", "18-49", "50-64", "65+"),
    create_calendar_vars = TRUE,
    lang                 = "pt"
  ) |>
  sus_data_aggregate(
    time_unit = "week",
    group_by  = c("uf", "age_group"),
    lang      = "pt"
  )

# --- 2. Raw climate + gap filling ---
df_clima_bruto <- sus_climate_inmet(
  uf       = c("RS", "SC", "PR"),
  year     = 2014:2022,
  variable = c("tair_min_c", "tair_max_c", "tair_dry_bulb_c"),
  lang     = "pt"
) |>
  sus_climate_fill_inmet(method = "random_forest", lang = "pt")

# --- 3. Cold wave detection ---
df_clima_cw <- sus_climate_compute_coldwaves(
  df             = df_clima_bruto,
  method         = c("WHO", "INMET"),
  baseline_start = "1981-01-01",
  baseline_end   = "2010-12-31",
  percentile     = 10,
  min_duration   = 3L,
  lang           = "pt"
)

# --- 4. Health + climate integration with cold wave flags ---
df_final <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  df_health  = df_saude,
  df_climate = df_clima_cw$daily_flag,
  strategy   = "threshold_exceedance",
  group_by   = c("uf", "age_group"),
  lang       = "pt"
)

Step-by-Step Explanation

sus_data_import() with system = "SIH" — Importing AIH records

For system = "SIH", the function downloads the RD (Admission Report) files of the SIH from the DATASUS FTP server. Each file contains one AIH per row, with admission date (DT_INTER), discharge date (DT_SAIDA), primary diagnosis (DIAG_PRINC), municipality of residence (MUNIC_RES), patient age (IDADE), sex (SEXO), and length of stay (DIAS_PERM). climasus4r uses DT_INTER (admission date) as the temporal reference, since it is the moment of initial contact with the health system — temporally closest to the climate exposure.

sus_data_filter_cid() on SIH — Respiratory diseases in AIH

In the SIH context, disease_group = "respiratory" selects AIH records whose DIAG_PRINC belongs to Chapter X of ICD-10 (J00–J99). The most frequent diagnoses for winter admissions in southern Brazil are: unspecified pneumonia (J18.9), acute bronchitis (J20), acute bronchiolitis (J21), COPD with acute exacerbation (J44.1), and acute respiratory failure (J96). The filter on DIAG_PRINC can be combined with filters on secondary diagnoses (DIAG_SEC*) to broaden case capture.

sus_data_create_variables() — Age groups and calendar variables

The age groups defined by the breaks c(0, 18, 50, 65, Inf) stratify risk by clinically relevant groups: pediatric and adolescent (< 18), young and middle-aged adult (18–49), pre-elderly (50–64), and elderly (65+). With create_calendar_vars = TRUE, the epiweek column is created for alignment with epidemiological surveillance bulletins, and the season column is created for controlling seasonality in models.

sus_climate_compute_coldwaves() — Automatic cold wave detection

This function is the cold-weather counterpart to sus_climate_compute_heatwaves() (Case Study 3). The percentile = 10 argument sets the threshold as the 10th percentile of the minimum temperature distribution over the reference period (1981–2010) — the exact complement of the 90th percentile used for heat. min_duration = 3L requires at least 3 consecutive days below the threshold to characterize a cold wave under the WHO criterion.

The INMET criterion uses a different logic: minimum temperature below (climatological monthly mean − 5°C) for at least 5 consecutive days. This criterion is based on INMET’s operational cold-wave alerts and is more restrictive than the WHO criterion — it detects only episodes of severe climatological deviation.

Output of sus_climate_compute_coldwaves(): The returned list has the same three elements as sus_climate_compute_heatwaves(): $events (discrete events with start date, end date, duration, and intensity), $daily_flag (daily dataset with cw_who_flag and cw_inmet_flag), and $annual_summary (annual cold wave summary by state).

WHO vs. INMET differences for cold waves

Criterion Reference variable Threshold Minimum duration
WHO Minimum temperature < P10 (1981–2010) 3 consecutive days
INMET Minimum temperature < monthly mean − 5°C 5 consecutive days

The WHO criterion is more suitable for population-level epidemiological studies because it captures relative variation with respect to local climatology — a day of 8°C in Porto Alegre has a different impact than a day of 8°C in Curitiba, and both are evaluated relative to their own climatological normal. The INMET criterion is more suitable for operational surveillance and real-time alerts.

strategy = "threshold_exceedance" — Integration with event flags

The "threshold_exceedance" strategy performs a temporal join between the weekly hospitalization dataset and the cold wave $daily_flag. Since the health dataset is at weekly resolution and the climate dataset is at daily resolution, the function automatically aggregates the daily flags to the weekly level: a week receives cw_who_flag = 1 if at least one day of that week was classified as a cold-wave day under the WHO criterion.

Attention to temporal resolution: Aggregating daily flags to the weekly level implies a loss of information. For analyses that require daily precision (e.g., case-crossover with day-of-week stratification), keep the health dataset at daily resolution using time_unit = "day" in the aggregation step.

Expected Output

After running the pipeline, df_final is a climasus_df object with the following main columns:

Column Type Description
date_week Date First day of the epidemiological week
epiweek integer Epidemiological week number (1–53)
uf character State abbreviation (RS, SC, PR)
age_group factor Age group (< 18, 18–49, 50–64, 65+)
n_hospitalizations integer Weekly count of respiratory admissions
cw_who_flag integer Weekly cold wave flag (WHO criterion)
cw_inmet_flag integer Weekly cold wave flag (INMET criterion)
tair_min_c double Weekly mean minimum temperature (°C)

Next Steps

With the integrated weekly dataset, the statistical analyses most suited to this type of data are:

  • Case-crossover study stratified by month/year: an ideal epidemiological design for estimating the acute effect of cold waves on hospitalizations, automatically controlling for long-period factors (seasonality, trend, day of week). See the tutorial Case-Crossover and ITS Analysis.
  • Attributable mortality/morbidity analysis: estimating the number of excess hospitalizations attributable to cold waves each year, with uncertainty intervals via bootstrapping. See the tutorial Attributable Mortality.
  • DLNM modeling: temperature-hospitalization exposure-response function with a lag distribution from 0 to 21 days, allowing assessment of the lag between cold exposure and the peak in admissions. See the tutorial DLNM Modeling.

References

Gasparrini, A., Guo, Y., Hashizume, M., et al. (2015). Mortality risk attributable to high and low ambient temperature: a multicountry observational study. Lancet, 386(9991), 369–375.

Eccles, R. (2002). An explanation for the seasonality of acute upper respiratory tract viral infections. Acta Otolaryngologica, 122(2), 183–191.

Perkins, S. E., & Alexander, L. V. (2013). On the measurement of heat waves. Journal of Climate, 26(13), 4500–4517.

WHO & WMO (2015). Heatwaves and Health: Guidance on Warning-System Development. Geneva: World Health Organization.

Brasil, Ministério da Saúde (2022). SIH — Sistema de Informações Hospitalares do SUS. Brasília: DATASUS. Available at: https://datasus.saude.gov.br/
